## Overview

This project builds a search engine over a corpus of arXiv malware-classification
papers, implementing and comparing seven retrieval methods head-to-head:
**BM25 → dense (SPECTER2) → hybrid (RRF) → cross-encoder rerank → late-interaction
(ColBERT via Qdrant) → k-means cluster-filtered search → generative retrieval
(a trained query→semantic-ID model)**.

Every method is evaluated on the same 40-query, LLM-judged relevance-labeled
eval set, using the same NDCG@10 / MRR metrics, and benchmarked on the same
latency harness. The goal was not just to build each technique, but to
honestly report where each one wins, where it loses, and why — including
findings that didn't come out the way theory alone would predict.

Code: [github.com/vinayhpandya/search-algorithms](https://github.com/vinayhpandya/search-algorithms)

## Corpus and Setup

- **Domain**: arXiv papers on malware classification (`cs.CR`, `cs.LG`, `cs.CV`
  categories), collected via the `arxiv` client library across 16 search
  queries, deduplicated
- **Enrichment**: citation counts from Semantic Scholar (used later as an
  LTR feature)
- **Index**: OpenSearch, single-node local Docker setup — chosen because it
  supports BM25 and k-NN vector search natively in one engine, letting
  lexical and semantic search share the same index and fuse without
  cross-system round trips
- **Scope decision**: abstract-only (no full-text PDFs), to keep the repo
  small and the project achievable in a weekend — noted as future work

## Methodology: Evaluation

### Relevance labeling

Manually labeling enough query-paper pairs for a meaningful eval set (857+
pairs across 40 queries) isn't realistic by hand in the available time.
Instead:

1. A **researcher** LLM rates each pair 0/1/2 with a rationale
2. A **critic** LLM reviews the researcher's rating and either confirms or
   overrides it — final label = critic's call
3. A **human spot-check** on a stratified sample (~65 pairs, weighted toward
   researcher/critic disagreements) validates the LLM labels

This is standard practice for evaluating relevance judgments at scale (the
same logic behind TREC-style IR evaluation and industry search-quality
teams checking LLM/crowd-worker judgments) — not a shortcut.

**Known calibration issue**: only ~3% of labeled pairs were rated "not
relevant" (0). Because candidate pools are built from real search results
(already topically adjacent to the query), the researcher/critic prompts
turned out lenient about what counts as irrelevant. This doesn't invalidate
the labels — NDCG@10 still discriminates well since it weights label=2 three
times as heavily as label=1 — but it does mean **MRR at the standard
threshold (label ≥ 1) saturates near 1.0 for every method** and carries no
signal. Reporting **MRR at threshold ≥ 2** ("how often is the very best
result found immediately") restored real discrimination between methods
without needing to relabel anything. (A tighter, binary relevance rubric was
designed as a follow-up fix but not run before this writeup — noted under
Future Work.)

### Metrics

- **NDCG@10**: rewards ranking highly-relevant results near the top;
  uses the full graded (0/1/2) label
- **MRR(≥2)**: reciprocal rank of the first *highly* relevant result — the
  metric that actually discriminates given this corpus's label distribution
- **Latency**: mean / p50 / p95 across 40 queries, local machine, no GPU

## Results: Retrieval Quality

| Method | NDCG@10 | MRR(≥1) | MRR(≥2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BM25             | 0.9003 | 1.0000 | 0.5969 |
| Dense            | 0.9026 | 1.0000 | 0.5763 |
| Hybrid           | 0.9142 | 1.0000 | 0.7261 |
| Rerank           | 0.9131 | 1.0000 | 0.7504 |
| Late-interaction | 0.9003 | 1.0000 | 0.6951 |
| Semantic ID (k-means, cluster-filtered) | 0.9624 | 0.9625 | 0.2744 |
| Generative (RQ-VAE + trained query→ID model) | 0.9005 | 1.0000 | 0.2432 |

### Reading the core four methods

**Dense underperforms BM25 on MRR(≥2)** (0.5763 vs 0.5969) despite
near-identical NDCG@10 — SPECTER2 embeddings surface broadly topical
neighbors well, but are less precise than exact keyword matching at
pinpointing the single best match at rank 1.

**Hybrid and rerank both correct for this**, each clearly outperforming
either input alone on MRR(≥2) — real evidence of fusion and reranking doing
genuine work, not just reshuffling noise.

**Late-interaction lands between dense and hybrid** (MRR≥2 = 0.6951) —
consistent with the theoretical expectation that token-level (MaxSim)
matching captures finer-grained relevance than single-vector cosine
similarity, without needing full cross-attention.

**Rerank is the best quality by both metrics** — expected, since a
cross-encoder sees the full query and document jointly via cross-attention
(strictly more expressive than any similarity-metric-based method here),
at the cost of only being feasible on a pre-filtered shortlist, never the
whole corpus.

### Two different semantic-ID-based methods, two different stories

Both remaining rows use "semantic IDs" but are otherwise unrelated methods,
worth not conflating:

- **Semantic ID (k-means)**: a two-level k-means clustering over SPECTER2
  embeddings, used to pre-filter/organize the corpus (IVF-style). Highest
  NDCG@10 of all seven methods (0.9624) but by far the lowest MRR(≥2)
  (0.2744) — it reliably finds *something* topically adjacent, but rarely
  the single best paper. A fixed, non-learned clustering, not a retrieval
  model in its own right.
- **Generative retrieval**: a genuinely trained model (RQ-VAE + query→ID
  decoder, detailed below) that predicts a semantic ID directly from the
  query text and looks up matching papers — the actual "generative
  retrieval" paradigm this project set out to test.

## Generative Retrieval: What Was Actually Built

Beyond the six baseline methods above, a from-scratch generative retrieval
pipeline was implemented, following the two-stage design used in
TIGER-style semantic ID systems:

**Stage 1 — RQ-VAE.** A small encoder/decoder (MLP, 768→512→256→32) with a
2-level residual vector quantizer (16 codewords/level, EMA codebook updates,
dead-code reset) trained on SPECTER2 embeddings to produce a hierarchical
2-digit semantic ID per paper (`[coarse, fine]`). Trained on the full
194-paper corpus; qualitative inspection showed genuinely topic-coherent
clusters (e.g. one cluster grouped five adversarial-malware-attack papers,
another grouped five malware-classification-methods papers).

**Stage 2 — query-to-ID model.** Since no real user queries exist, ~1,940
synthetic (query, semantic_id) pairs were generated via LLM (10 queries per
paper, mixing keyword-close and oblique natural-language phrasings). A
frozen MiniLM sentence encoder + small 2-layer transformer decoder was
trained to autoregressively predict a paper's semantic ID digit-by-digit
from a query, with beam search at inference time. Train/val split was done
**by paper**, not by row, to prevent different phrasings of the same
paper's queries leaking across the split.

**Evaluation methodology.** The trained model was wired into the same eval
harness as the other six methods: for each of the 40 eval queries, beam
search produces ranked candidate semantic IDs, each ID's matching papers
are pulled in beam order to build a ranked top-10 list, and that list is
scored with the same NDCG@10/MRR machinery and LLM-judged labels used
throughout.

**Result: a clear, honest negative finding.** Training showed a real
generalization gap — training exact-match accuracy climbed to 36% while
validation exact-match stayed near 2–5%, i.e. the model was memorizing
training-set query phrasings rather than learning to generalize across
topics. This is directly reflected in the eval numbers: NDCG@10 (0.9005)
looks reasonable only because the label set skews lenient (see calibration
note above), while MRR(≥2) (0.2432) — the metric that actually measures
whether the *single best* paper is found — is among the weakest of all
seven methods. The most likely cause, and the most actionable finding: 194
papers (165 after the train/val split) is simply too little topic diversity
for a 256-way discrete prediction task to generalize from — an architecture
problem this isn't; a data-scale problem it is. Scaling to a larger corpus
(e.g. the ~100k-paper ML-ArXiv-Papers subset) is the natural next step to
test that hypothesis directly.

## Latency

Mean / p50 / p95 across 40 queries, local machine, no GPU:

| Method | Mean (ms) | P50 (ms) | P95 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BM25 | 2.7 | 2.6 | 3.3 |
| Late-interaction | 12.6 | 12.3 | 16.0 |
| Generative | 20.4 | 20.0 | 23.9 |
| Semantic ID (k-means) | 30.5 | 30.4 | 36.0 |
| Dense | 42.7 | 42.7 | 48.0 |
| Hybrid | 59.6 | 59.4 | 64.8 |
| Rerank | 187.8 | 186.8 | 200.9 |

BM25 is fastest by a wide margin, as expected — no model inference at all.
Generative retrieval lands in the middle of the pack: slower than BM25 and
late-interaction, but notably faster than dense search despite also
requiring a forward pass, since the query encoder here (frozen MiniLM) is
far smaller than SPECTER2, and lookup after ID prediction is a cheap
dictionary access rather than a k-NN search over the full corpus. Rerank is
the clear latency outlier, consistent with cross-encoders' cost scaling
with the number of candidates scored, not just query size — the tradeoff
that pairs it with a cheap first-stage retriever in practice rather than
running it corpus-wide.

## Future Work

- **Rerun evaluation under a binary (0/1), query-specific relevance rubric**
  — designed to fix the labeling calibration issue described above, but not
  executed before this writeup.
- **Scale the corpus** (e.g. to the ~100k-paper ML-ArXiv-Papers subset) to
  directly test whether generative retrieval's weak MRR(≥2) is a data-scale
  problem, as the evidence here suggests, rather than an architectural one.
- **Hypencoders** Testing a small Qnet and hype-encoder based network, want to see how fast it is to train and how well the NDCG scores are
- **Full-text PDFs and a RAG QA layer** on top of the retrieval stack —
  scoped out from the very beginning to keep this project achievable in
  the available time.
